look_here_first: FIRST photograph the UPPER FACE of an actual mature leaf or white-margined BRACT. *Euphorbia marginata* usually has a GLABROUS (mostly smooth, hairless) UPPER blade; stems, peduncles, lower midribs and capsules may STILL be hairy. Second, compare the LARGEST fully developed showy BRACTS: usually relatively BROAD elliptic/obovate rather than the very long linear-to-narrowly-oblanceolate bracts of *E. bicolor*. Both species can look just as white, and smaller secondary bracts of *marginata* may be narrow. 'More frosting' or 'even white borders' is NOT a reliable field key. What looks like large white flower petals are white-margined MODIFIED LEAVES (bracts), along with small white cyathial-gland appendages. Hays/Travis/Kerr project native-range PASS stays in place.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Euphorbia: milky latex and a cyathium instead of an ordinary petaled flower. The conspicuous white areas are primarily bracts plus gland appendages.
morphology_keys.growth_form: Annual, erect herb with a conspicuously white-topped flowering canopy.
morphology_keys.leaves: Distal leaves and bracts become conspicuously white-margined; the showiest upper bracts are relatively broad.
morphology_keys.pubescence: Upper leaf surfaces are mostly glabrous. Hairiness can still occur on lower surfaces, along the midrib, peduncles, cyathia, ovary, and capsule, so 'the whole plant is hairless' is not a safe rule.
morphology_keys.bracts: Largest white-margined bracts are generally broader, commonly elliptic to obovate, rather than the long narrow linear-to-narrowly-oblanceolate bracts of E. bicolor.
morphology_keys.cyathium: Flower-like cyathia bear pale glands with conspicuous white appendages.
morphology_keys.fruit: Three-lobed capsule, conspicuously hairy; detailed Williamson treatment gives capsules about 4.5–5 × 7–7.5 mm.
morphology_keys.seed: Seeds about 4.5 × 3 mm in the detailed Williamson treatment, with minute tuberculate/netlike surface patterning.
best_field_traits: Native to target zone under existing Hays, Travis and Kerr county records; no need to change this project's PASS.
Annual erect/taprooted plant, white-topped canopy, often 30–85 cm; height does not separate it from *E. bicolor*.
Stem leaves alternate and relatively BROAD ovate to elliptic; showiest distal white-margined bracts mostly elliptic to obovate rather than extremely slender.
Upper faces of mature leaves/bracts commonly GLABROUS, even when the stem or under-leaf midrib has hairs.
Smaller inner inflorescence bracts CAN be narrow; don't ID by one tiny secondary bract.
White bract margins and little white cyathial gland appendages are different organs, neither ordinary flower petals.
The actual Euphorbia reproductive unit is a small cyathium containing reduced male and female flowers.
Fruit is a three-lobed hairy capsule and does NOT by itself separate it from the also hairy *E. bicolor*.
Bract whiteness, size, and apparent 'frosty' versus 'patchy' color are unreliable if used alone.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Against E. bicolor, use two linked characters: E. marginata is generally broader-bracted and glabrous on the upper leaf/bract surfaces; E. bicolor is narrower-bracted and conspicuously hairy above.

crew_glossary.upper_adaxial_face: The TOP of a mature leaf/bract that is facing upward in the photo, not the underside and not the hairy STEM.
crew_glossary.glabrous: Without obvious hairs; this is best examined with a hand lens and angled light, not assumed from an ordinary cellphone photo.
crew_glossary.upper_bract: Modified leaf near cyathium; often white around edges, still a LEAF, not a petal.
crew_glossary.cyathium: Cup-like inflorescence of reduced flowers, with nectar glands and often white appendages.
crew_glossary.elliptic_obovate: Relatively BROAD blade, widest mid-blade or towards tip, rather than long strap-like blade.

field_photo_steps: 1. Full specimen photo showing erect annual and entire canopy.
2. Get TWO examples of largest mature white-edged upper bracts laid flat at matching ruler scale.
3. Macro the UPPER FACE of the same bract using side lighting; show little/no hairs where bicolor would be conspicuously hairy.
4. Photograph separately any very hairy STEM to explain why hair LOCATION matters.
5. If fruit present, get a calibrated close-up of the real hairy THREE-LOBED capsule and separate it from smaller cyathia.
6. Compare against *E. bicolor* source photo at the same maturity, rather than white color pattern.
morphology_keys.ecology: Grasslands and disturbed open sites, commonly Central Texas. Do not assume ornamental forms represent Hays County wild provenance. Existing Hays native-range approval retained.
morphology_keys.latex_caution: White latex can irritate skin and eyes; do not deliberately break plants for a demonstration.

comparisons.key_distinctions: *E. marginata* = usually BROADER mature white-margined bracts + mostly GLABROUS UPPER bract/leaf face. *E. bicolor* = LONG NARROW strap-like bracts + conspicuous UPPER-SURFACE hairs. Stems of marginata can be hairy. Both species may have narrow secondary bracts and heavy white display. Location of hairs, not overall fuzz, is critical.

field_comparison_matrix.marginata: Broad elliptic/obovate (smaller secondary may be narrow)

comparisons.uncertainty: Without an upper-blade hair macro and mature bract comparison, keep an uncertain specimen as Euphorbia bicolor–marginata group.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Snow-on-the-mountain: broad bracts, then inspect TOP of leaf
steps: Look for the larger BROAD white-edged bracts, and ignore any little narrow secondary ones as a stand-alone character.
Remember white 'petals' are modified BRACTS and tiny gland APPENDAGES; the actual flowers are within small cyathia.
Observe hairy stems in the NPS photo, next to the broad GREEN leaf: hair on stem does not mean hair on upper leaf.
Turn a true mature upper leaf/bract TOP upwards under strong light. Smooth/glabrous upper face supports marginata; upper-face hairs + very long narrow bracts favor bicolor.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Broad mature white-margined bracts + smooth TOP face = *E. marginata*. Photo shows shape and a hairy stem, but a calibrated upper-face hair close-up is still pending.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Do NOT claim the whole *E. marginata* plant is hairless. Do NOT rely on neat white rims versus patchy white.
